issues.legal_issue: Delegated authority to regulate royalties for minor minerals is sufficiently guided and is not an unbridled delegation of legislative power.
material_facts: The State fixed and enhanced royalties for minor minerals under authority delegated by Parliament.

The governing framework stated the purpose of regulating and developing mines and minerals and included provisions addressing mineral conservation, environmental protection, lease termination, and prevention of illegal mining.
The framework also required State rules and notifications to be placed before the State Legislature.
issues.conclusion: The delegation to the State is not excessive or unbridled; statutory purposes, provisions, and legislative scrutiny provide sufficient guidance and checks.
issues.legal_principle: Section 15(1) of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, read with Section 15(1-A), confers rule-making power concerning minor minerals. The guidance is found in the Act’s purpose and scheme, the illustrative matters for rulemaking, relevant provisions including Sections 4-A, 17, 18 and 23-C, and the requirement in Section 28(3) to place State rules and notifications before the State Legislature. D.K. Trivedi & Sons v. State of Gujarat held that the power under Section 15 is guided and includes power to alter royalty and dead rent. The Court also relied on the principles concerning guided delegation and statutory purpose in Municipal Corporation of Delhi v. Birla Cotton, Spinning and Weaving Mills, Corporation of Calcutta v. Liberty Cinema, Bhatnagar & Co. v. Union of India, and State of Tamil Nadu v. Hind Stone; it applied the purposive approach in Heydon’s Case and authorities following it.

rule.if: minor_mineral_royalty_rulemaking_case and state_received_delegated_rulemaking_power and statutory_policy_guides_mineral_regulation and related_rules_and_controls_exist and legislative_scrutiny_is_provided

predicates.minor_mineral_royalty_rulemaking_case: The proceeding concerns rules or notifications governing royalty for minor minerals.
predicates.state_received_delegated_rulemaking_powe: The State exercised rule-making authority delegated to it by the legislature.
predicates.statutory_policy_guides_mineral_regulati: The governing framework states a policy of regulating and developing mineral resources.
predicates.related_rules_and_controls_exist: The governing framework contains related provisions addressing matters such as conservation, environmental protection, and mining operations.
predicates.legislative_scrutiny_is_provided: The governing framework requires State rules or notifications to be placed before the State Legislature.

issues.definition: When a proceeding concerns State rulemaking on minor-mineral royalties, and the State acts under delegated authority within a statutory framework that guides mineral regulation and provides related controls and legislative scrutiny, the delegation is guided and valid.

issues.legal_issue: The State’s authority to fix royalties for minor minerals is not limited by the rate stated in the residuary entry of the Second Schedule.
material_facts: The challenged notifications enhanced royalties for minor minerals.
The challengers argued that the residuary entry in the Second Schedule imposed a maximum rate based on the sale price at the pit’s mouth.
The Act excluded the provisions governing the Second Schedule’s royalty rates from their application to minor minerals.
issues.conclusion: The State is not confined to the rate in the residuary entry of the Second Schedule when fixing royalties for minor minerals.
issues.legal_principle: Section 14 excludes Sections 5 to 13, including Section 9, from applying to minor minerals. The Second Schedule sets royalty rates through Section 9 and therefore does not impose its residuary rate as a ceiling for minor minerals. D.K. Trivedi & Sons v. State of Gujarat did not hold that the State’s power under Section 15 is restricted by that entry; its discussion of Sections 4 to 12 identified matters available as guidance, not binding limits on the State’s power. The Court also relied on Section 15 and the distinction between minor minerals and other minerals in the Act’s scheme.

predicates.minor_mineral_royalty_case: The proceeding concerns the rate of royalty fixed for minor minerals.
predicates.residuary_schedule_rate_applies_to_other: The residuary royalty rate forms part of the rate scheme for minerals other than minor minerals.
predicates.statutory_exclusion_removes_minor_minera: The governing framework excludes minor minerals from the provisions that apply the scheduled royalty-rate scheme.

issues.definition: When royalty is fixed for minor minerals that are excluded from the scheduled rate scheme, the State’s rate is not limited by that scheme’s residuary rate.

issues.legal_issue: Failure to place a State notification before the State Legislature as required does not invalidate the notification when the placement requirement is directory.
material_facts: One of the challenged notifications was required to be placed before the State Legislature.
The notification had been referred to in departmental administrative reports, but the Court found that it had not actually been placed before the Legislature as required.
The governing provision required placement but did not make the notification subject to legislative approval or modification.
issues.conclusion: The omission to place the notification did not invalidate it; the State was directed to place it before the Legislature at the earliest and to comply with the requirement in future.
issues.legal_principle: Section 28(3) of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, requires State rules and notifications to be laid before the State Legislature. Unlike Section 28(1), it does not provide for legislative approval or modification. The Court held that placement nevertheless operates as a check on the State and is not futile, but that the requirement is directory, so non-placement does not invalidate the notification. It relied on Atlas Cycle Industries Ltd. v. State of Haryana, which treated a comparable laying requirement as directory.

predicates.validity_challenge_to_state_delegated_no: The proceeding challenges the validity of a notification made by the State under delegated authority.
predicates.notification_was_not_formally_placed_bef: The State did not formally place the notification before the Legislature as required.
predicates.placement_requirement_is_directory: The requirement to place the notification before the Legislature does not make legislative approval a condition of the notification’s validity.

issues.definition: When a challenged State notification was not formally placed before the Legislature but the placement requirement is directory, the notification remains valid despite non-placement.

issues.legal_issue: The challenged royalty enhancement is not arbitrary or otherwise illegal when the record does not establish arbitrariness or excessiveness.
material_facts: The challengers asserted that the increased royalty was excessive and difficult to pay.
The Court found no material in the writ petition establishing that the enhancement was arbitrary, excessive, or confiscatory.
The record showed that the State had increased the royalty only four times over the period considered and had not increased it for six years before the decision.
issues.conclusion: On the material presented, the enhancement could not be held arbitrary or otherwise illegal.
issues.legal_principle: A possibility that delegated power may be abused does not itself invalidate its exercise; a challenge to an allegedly arbitrary or excessive exercise must be supported by a specific plea and material based on the circumstances of the case. The Court applied this approach alongside its conclusion in D.K. Trivedi & Sons v. State of Gujarat that a substantial increase is not invalid merely because of its size.

predicates.appeal_challenges_royalty_enhancement: The proceeding challenges an increase in royalty imposed by the State.
predicates.no_case_specific_material_establishes_ar: The challenger provides no case-specific material showing that the enhancement was arbitrary, excessive, or confiscatory.
predicates.increases_were_infrequent: The record shows that the State increased the royalty infrequently and had left it unchanged for a substantial period before the challenge.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges a royalty enhancement, the challenger supplies no case-specific material establishing arbitrariness, and increases were infrequent, the enhancement is not arbitrary or illegal.
